newsitem.title: UK: COMMODITIES - Cocoa prices power higher, coffee sags.
newsitem.headline: COMMODITIES - Cocoa prices power higher, coffee sags.

text.p: Speculative fever continued to grip world cocoa prices on Tuesday, driving them to fresh nine-year highs in New York as the market fed off a strong fundamental picture and an even stronger technical outlook.
"The buying is feeding on itself," one trader in London said of the current two-day rally, which began after a smaller-than-expected reported rise in net speculative long positions in New York.

The market had been bracing for a strong sell-off if the figures had come in above forecast. Large fund buying led the charge in New York on Monday amid bullish technical indicators and reflecting the possibility of a lower 1997/98 crop.

On the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York cocoa traded as high as $1,722 a tonne on Tuesday on the September contract before settling back to $1,703 a tonne. London's September contract closed up 11 stg at 1,141 stg a tonne.

The latest rally has propelled the price up some 15 percent since early June, fuelled by preliminary crop forecasts out of the Ivory Coast, the world's largest producer, which have pointed to a reduced 1997/98 harvest.

Talk of output being hit by dry weather from a developing El Nino weather pattern has also aided the run up, although some traders caution that it is still too early to predict a crop shortage next season.
Coffee, on the other hand, continued its recent slump after coming under pressure on Monday from a private forecast that predicted Brazil's 1997/98 harvest to be well above the country's estimate.

Continuing mild weather in Brazil's coffee belt also dampened sentiment as June and July are the main damaging frost months. The latest forecasts show no harmful cold there over the next week. London robusta coffee futures ended the day down $30 on the September contract at $1,815 per tonne.

Elsewhere in the commodity markets, copper suffered a further fall on speculative liquidation as signs that the tight supply situation was easing. Zinc reversed much of Monday's run-up to slip below the $1,400 a tonne level.
In precious metals, gold traded sideways after the mild boost it received from comments by the Japanese Prime Minister that his country had considered selling U.S. Treasuries and buying gold fizzled.
Traders said the long-term outlook remained negative. Bullion ended the day in London at $338.75 ounce versus $338.45 on Monday.

Crude oil climbed slightly on follow-through strength from Monday although dealers reported little concern about the on-going OPEC meeting in Vienna, where the current output quota of 25.03 million barrels per day is expected to be rolled over.
Renewed tensions between the United Nations and Iraq have provided a bullish backdrop for oil and helped push prices through important technical resistance levels at around $18.00 a barrel.
Bellwether London Brent for August delivery was up three cents at $18.02.
